title: Hopps: Leveraging Sparsity to Accelerate Automata Processing
problem: Automata processing (AP) workloads execute many finite state machines (FSMs) in parallel over streaming symbol data, but existing AP accelerators suffer poor utilization because most FSMs are inactive (in a non-matching state) for any given input symbol. The irregular, state-dependent activation pattern makes it hard to exploit spatial parallelism efficiently.
motivation: Pattern matching against large rule sets (e.g., network intrusion detection, genomics scanning) demands high-throughput AP, but the inherent sparsity of active FSM transitions wastes memory bandwidth and compute cycles in existing DRAM- and SRAM-based AP engines.
method: The key insight is that on each incoming symbol, only a small subset of the state machines actually need to process it—most are idle. Hopps tracks which state machines are active at any moment using a compact bitmap (a compressed list of which machines are 'turned on') and skips over the inactive ones entirely. It also arranges the memory using tiled SRAM storage, so that state-transition rules for active machines are fetched in batches rather than one at a time, which cuts down the amount of data pulled from slower off-chip memory in proportion to how many machines are actually active.
key_novelty: Hopps is the first automata processing accelerator to completely eliminate wasted processing on inactive state machines by using a bitmap to track which machines are active on each input symbol.
contributions: Characterization of sparsity in AP workloads showing that the fraction of active FSMs per symbol step is typically low.
A sparsity-aware hardware architecture (Hopps) that uses activation bitmaps to skip inactive FSMs and reduce memory traffic.
Evaluation demonstrating significant speedup and energy reduction over prior AP accelerators on data analytics and scientific computing workloads.
limitations: Not discussed in the abstract; full quantitative results unavailable without full text.
